analysis.investment_thesis: Fabtech is a tiny (INR 270 Cr mcap), lumpy turnkey engineering shop for pharma cleanrooms with decent headline ROCE (21.2%) but poor earnings quality — FY25 OCF of just INR 3 Cr against net profit of INR 13 Cr, and essentially zero free cash flow. Invert: project-based businesses with working-capital-heavy receivables, no visible moat, and a one-year-old listing are precisely the kind of thing I avoid at 27.6x earnings.
key_strengths: ROCE 21.2% and ROE 18.1% — above cost of capital on reported numbers.
Low debt (INR 10 Cr vs INR 95 Cr equity); balance sheet not leveraged.
Niche exposure to pharma/biotech capex tailwind; revenue CAGR 11% over 5 years.
key_risks: FCF/NI abysmal — FY25 FCF ~0 on INR 13 Cr PAT; earnings not converting to cash.
Commoditized turnkey fabrication, no moat, no switching costs, no pricing power.
red_flags: 5-yr cumulative OCF ~INR 21 Cr vs cumulative PAT ~INR 36 Cr — cash-flow gap typical of EPC.
Microcap with zero FII ownership; limited institutional scrutiny.
Recent IPO (equity 52→95 Cr in FY25); unproven capital allocation of fresh INR 43 Cr.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Applying inversion: what kills returns in a business like this? Working capital blowups on fixed-price turnkey contracts, a single bad project, loss of key clients, or a downcycle in pharma capex. The cash-flow statement already whispers the warning — despite revenue growing from 97 to 150 Cr and PAT doubling to 13 Cr, FY25 operating cash flow stayed at just 3 Cr. That is the signature of receivables and inventory soaking up profits, classic of EPC/turnkey vendors. A 27.6x multiple on earnings that don't translate to cash is not a margin of safety; it's the opposite.

The ROCE headline is flattering but earned on a small asset base, and the business just ballooned equity ~80% via fresh capital it has yet to deploy productively (INR 26 Cr investing outflow in FY25, CWIP still zero). Cleanroom engineering for pharma is a real niche, but fragmented and commoditized at the fabrication layer — no pricing power, no switching costs, no compounding flywheel. Fails my test of "a wonderful business at a fair price." Pass.
